you just explained it yourself?
Since the highest bid is 9992 and the lowest ask is only 10008, I still don't get how the trade occurred. Im sorry am I missing something?
The bid at 9992 is a resting order, a bot sent a market sell that hit it. The prices csv shows the book, the trades csv shows when someone crosses into it.

You can generalize this argument, actually. It is true for every single exchange that `bid < ask` for all products (Apple, Microsoft, etc.). So if you think a trade occurs when bid >= ask, there would never be any trades on any exchange ever 😉
Yet there are many trades every second, therefore trades don't happen when bid >= ask in the order book 😉

The bids and asks you see in the order book are, as MirkovicDev said, 'resting', waiting for someone to 'hit'. If I'm bidding 9992, my offer is in the order book, but if MirkovicDev then says "I'll sell for 9992", he sells it to me, and my bid is deleted from the order book (so you never saw ask <= bid in the order book, that happens behind the scenes)

In general. A colossal problem occurs, part of it is indeed "share your strategy by accident"

But. Say I write up a code that exploits the following phenomenon.

On every 1st monday of the month, after a financial report. The probability of a positive return is 75%

Now someone else won't have that exact idea, but will notice the following instead.

If a financial report is published and the revenue is above expectation, the probability of the next weeks returns being positive is 65%.
By chance those two overlap in part by execution
So both, say trader A and trader B will overlap their executions and profits by somewhat of a chance.
Now there are also significant problems with sharing the same alpha, but all of this ends up occuring as we are all looking at roughly the same phenomenon and end up with roughly the same behaviours.

This is why companies like Jane Street are looking into mean field games as well.

Where if we have the same idea and know one strategy is maximum profitable, it might actually be smarter to choose a less profitable strategy, because it is less crowded

Yeah, one strategy I have been told by multiple individuals in the industry now is.

Implement something like 100 strategies that are slight variations of the same phenomenon, that way you will capture more of the same alpha, while your competition is also trying to crowd you out.

of course there are the execution algorithms executed to capture your actual alpha. But it is a genuine idea to spread out your order, strategy and pnl on something like 100 accounts controlled by one set of algos

Hey everyone! First time doing Prosperity and really enjoying it. I've been digging deep into the R0 data and wanted to share some observations and ask a few questions — purely trying to learn here, not looking for anyone to share their secret sauce 😄

**1. Spoofing signal in TOMATOES**
I ran some analysis on the L2/L3 order book and found that fake buy walls (large bids in L2/L3) predict a price DROP ~96% of the time (~3pts in 5 ticks), and fake sell walls predict a price RISE ~97% of the time. The statistical significance is insane (p-value ~10⁻⁵⁶). But when I tried to actually monetize this — whether through aggressive taking against the spoof or adjusting my making quotes — the PnL impact was basically zero because the expected move (~3pts) is smaller than the half-spread (~7pts). Has anyone found a way to actually profit from this signal, or is it one of those "looks amazing on paper but useless in practice" things?

**2. Overfitting to the final price move**
I noticed that a big chunk of my TOMATOES PnL comes from being accidentally long when the price happens to rally at the end of the day. My market maker naturally accumulates long inventory over time (more NPC sells hitting my bid than NPC buys lifting my ask), so my PnL curve basically tracks the price. If the final move had been down instead of up, my PnL would tank. Is this something others are seeing too? It feels like a lot of the backtest PnL is just luck on the terminal price rather than actual alpha. Curious how people are thinking about this.

3. Capturing Large Fills vs Partials
Looking at the leaderboard, some top entries have massive average fill sizes. Looking at the CSV data, I see NPC liquidity often sits around 15-30 units per level. However, when I quote passively, I frequently only get hit for small partial fills (my current avg fill is sitting at ~4.32) before the price moves away, or I get fully filled only right before getting run over by a toxic trend. For those with high average fill sizes: is this usually achieved by aggressively taking those 20+ lot levels, or is there a trick to getting fully filled on the passive side without absorbing toxic flow?

Would love to hear anyone's thoughts on any of these. Just trying to understand the game better! 🙏

**⚠️ DO NOT opt into rankings on prosperity.equirag.com**

This is a third-party visualizer (not official IMC). If you enable "Opt Into Rankings" and upload a raw .log file, your **entire log is sent to and stored on their server**. Their own UI says it's retained for "verification, future revalidation, and fraud review."

**What's in your .log file:**
- Every order you placed (prices, volumes, timing)
- Your PnL curve and position at every tick
- Your algorithm's debug prints (fair value estimates, quote prices, signal triggers)
- Your serialized traderData (persisted state between ticks)

Anyone with server access can reverse-engineer your strategy from this.

**Safe usage:** Upload WITHOUT opt-in → data stays in your browser (client-side JS only). Verify by checking your browser's Network tab during upload — no requests should go to their API.

**Rule: Never share raw .log files outside the team.**

In general, IMC cares a lot about Sharpe (+ scalability), arguably even more than PnL. If you make final PnL = $1m but you have volatility of PnL = $10m, then your strategy is getting killed immediately by both management and the risk team, while PnL of $1m is pretty nice.

In fact, places like Millennium (top hedge fund) care almost exclusively about Sharpe ratios. A lot of teams there have a 3-5% max drawdown rule, and if they violate it, half of their capital is taken away. Thus, Sharpe is key since you want to minimize PnL volatility to avoid a max drawdown of >5%.

In Prosperity, final PnL is the metric to determine the winners and leaderboard, but Sharpe is still very important (and I'd recommend everyone to compute it) to assess how likely your strategy is to hold out-of-sample during the LONG (final) run. During testing on our side, there were some traders that worked really well for in-sample (SHORT run of 100k timesteps) but terrible for out-of-sample (LONG run of 1m timestep).

the core principle of Prosperity is Market Making, that is, crossing the gap between buyers and sellers. If all the buyers are only willing to buy at 9992 and all the sellers are only willing to sell at 10008, no trades will happen! However, there are always a few "market takers" who are willing to buy at suboptimal prices. Our goal is to get them to buy from *us* instead of other market makers (this can be done, for example, by saying you'll buy for 9993 and sell at 10007, making yours the best deal for the market taker)
start with emeralds, and implement this basic market making strategy, you will be ahead of the claude-spamming competition already
